Migration Amendment (Australia's Engagement in the Pacific and Other Measures) Bill 2023
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would change the main family law Act to make separation less complicated and focus on what is best for children.
It would rewrite the part of the Act that deals with parenting orders, add rules for hearing children's views, and give courts a new power to stop repeated legal harassment.
The changes would also bring forward a review of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Act by two years.
Simplify the framework for deciding parenting arrangements and children's best interests.
Allow children to express their views to an Independent Children's Lawyer in appropriate cases.
Create a new court power to prevent systems abuse by stopping repetitive applications.
Better recognise Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children's cultural rights and kinship concepts.
Make the consequences of not following parenting orders clearer.
Introduce harmful proceedings orders to stop vexatious litigants filing without court permission.
Separating families, children, family courts, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.

The Schedule also repeals the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility and the mandatory consideration of certain times arrangements for parents. The Family Law Amendment (Information Sharing) Bill 2023 was moved to enhance information sharing between family law courts and state/territory child protection, police and firearms authorities, introducing new court orders for particulars and production of documents, and safeguards for sensitive information, with the aim of improving child safety and closing gaps between federal and state systems.

The Northern Australia Infrastructure Facility Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2023, the Infrastructure Australia Amendment (Independent Review) Bill 2023, the Family Law Amendment Bill 2023, the Family Law Amendment (Information Sharing) Bill 2023, and the Crimes and Other Legislation Amendment (Omnibus) Bill 2023 were referred to the Federation Chamber for further consideration at the adjournment of the debate on the second reading of each bill.

The coalition member argued the Family Law Amendment Bill 2023 contains untested solutions that could worsen outcomes for Australian families, opposing the repeal of the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility and raising concerns about enforcement, Indigenous children provisions, and independent children's lawyers.

The coalition supports the intent of many measures in the Family Law Amendment Bill 2023 but cannot support it without further scrutiny, citing concerns over practical impacts in remote areas, lack of consultation on a review date change for the Federal Circuit and Family Court merger, and inadequate testing of solutions. The coalition will back a committee inquiry to examine the bill before finalising its position.

The member moved amendments to the Family Law Amendment Bill 2023 requiring a reasonable attempt to consult on long‑term decisions, codifying the *Rice v Asplund* test for reopening final parenting orders before any hearing, and requiring a reasonable attempt to understand obligations as a defence to contravention. Further amendments sought to include family violence history and family violence orders as mandatory considerations, define repeated legal systems abuse as family violence, and add cultural‑linguistic background factors for children’s best interests. The government did not support the amendments, noting the bill would be referred to a committee.
This bill is part of a package that would create a $10 billion fund to boost social and affordable housing, and set up an independent advisory body on housing policy.
The fund would be managed by the Future Fund Board, with its earnings spent on housing for Indigenous communities, women, children, veterans, and other groups in need.
The bill would start on a day fixed by Proclamation, or six months after it receives Royal Assent, whichever comes first.
The bill would establish the Housing Australia Future Fund to provide a dedicated funding source for social and affordable housing.
The bill would create the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council as an independent body to advise the government on housing supply and affordability.
The bill would allocate $330 million to address acute housing needs over the fund's first five years.
The explanatory memorandum says the bill would affect people needing social or affordable housing, Indigenous communities, women, children, veterans, and the Future Fund Board.

The Selection of Bills Committee presented its first report of 2023, referring multiple bills to committees for inquiry, including the Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023 and related housing bills to the Economics Legislation Committee with a reporting date of 22 March. Senator McKim moved an unsuccessful amendment to extend that reporting date to 22 April, arguing the government's housing response is inadequate and a longer inquiry is needed to hear from renters and housing sector stakeholders.

The motion to change committee memberships was agreed, with Senator Faruqi replacing McKim on the Economics Legislation Committee for the Housing Australia Future Fund Bill inquiry, and McKim replacing Shoebridge on the Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee for the Migration Amendment (Evacuation to Safety) Bill inquiry. Senators Bilyk, Brockman, Payne, Shoebridge, Sterle and White were appointed to the National Anti-Corruption Commission Joint Statutory Committee.

The speaker argued that the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2022 and the Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023 are urgent election commitments that will rebuild manufacturing, create jobs, reduce imports, and lower social costs, and criticised opposition to the bills as politically and economically senseless.
Customs Tariff Amendment (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement Implementation) Bill 2021

The Customs Tariff Amendment (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement Implementation) Bill 2021 implements Australia's import tariff commitments under the RCEP by inserting a new schedule of duty rates, eliminating duties for most originating goods over time, and retaining customs duty on excise equivalent goods such as fuel, alcohol, tobacco and petroleum products.
Customs Amendment (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement Implementation) Bill 2021

The bill implements the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (RCEP), the world's largest free trade agreement covering 15 signatories including Australia, ASEAN, China, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea, which accounts for nearly 60% of Australia's trade and two-thirds of exports. The bill inserts rules of origin and document retention requirements into the Customs Act 1901.

The bill improves the operation of Australian government investment funds, including a new employment framework for the Future Fund Management Agency, a partial FOI exemption for investment documents, a fixed maximum annual disbursement of $650 million for the Medical Research Future Fund from 2022-23, and transferring Emergency Response Fund responsibility to the National Recovery and Resilience Agency.
Treasury Laws Amendment (COVID-19 Economic Response) Bill 2021

The bill extends tax-free treatment of state and territory COVID-19 business support grants into the 2021-22 income year and allows the ATO to share taxpayer information with Services Australia to prevent ineligible COVID-19 disaster payments.
Social Services Legislation Amendment (Strengthening Income Support) Bill 2021

The Social Services Legislation Amendment (Strengthening Income Support) Bill 2021 provides an additional $50 per fortnight to working-age payment recipients from 1 April, permanently increases the income-free area to $150 for JobSeeker and youth allowance, and extends several temporary pandemic measures until 30 June 2021, at an estimated cost of $9 billion.

The Agriculture Legislation Amendment (Streamlining Administration) Bill 2019 was introduced to authorise automated decision-making by computer programs for biosecurity and imported food decisions, aiming to improve efficiency amid threats like brown marmorated stink bug and African swine fever, with the Department of Agriculture processing 45,000 commercial cargo referrals monthly.

The Agriculture Legislation Amendment (Streamlining Administration) Bill 2019 provides a statutory basis for automated decision-making under the Biosecurity Act 2015 and Imported Food Control Act 1992, aiming to improve efficiency amid 45,000 monthly commercial cargo referrals and threats like African swine fever virus and khapra beetle.
